Dossier 1: state with school facility ban (birth certificate), no enforcement mechanism, second-highest tier of five tiers in July 2026 assessment, resident restrictions. Under parent 0.35. Anti-discrimination: no state statute but executive order for state employment and 33 municipal ordinances. So mild negative relative to parent, maybe slightly below parent: ~0.33.

Dossier 2: highly protective state — top bands, most protective, anti-discrimination since 2008 including public accommodations (visitor-facing), facilities access protected, hate crime covering gender identity, hate-crime conviction, gay panic abolished, refuge protections ("safe refuge" for people fleeing restrictive laws), document markers changeable with X. Operating protective machinery — rule 13: protective operating regimes raise score materially above parent average. So maybe 0.55-0.60. But national framework still applies (passport restrictions, entry screening) — those are parent-level. Parent 0.35; a genuinely protective state sits above. Considerations: national passport regime applies regardless; state-level facility protections; anti-discrimination covering public accommodations (traveller-facing). Under rule 12-ish, it's not a dependent territory but a division; still, national layer carries. Protective division should sit well above parent. I'd say 0.58.

Dossier 3: state removed gender identity from civil rights statutes (first to withdraw), 2026 law precluding stronger local protections, school facilities birth-certificate rule binding everyone on school grounds including visitors, listed in worst group in July 2026 assessment, 2023 care/sports bans, conversion therapy partly legal. That's worse than parent average. Facility rule for schools is limited scope though (school grounds). No adult public-restroom statute documented. Listed in "worst group" tier. So below parent: ~0.26-0.30. The withdrawal of anti-discrimination plus worst-tier grading. I'd say 0.27.

Dossier 4: state with statutory protections (2020 civil rights covering gender identity in public accommodations), hate crime covering gender identity, panic defence repeal, X marker on licenses, birth certificate change easier, sodomy repealed, low-risk group in July 2026 assessment, youth-targeting policies unlikely to extend to adults. Restriction: 2023 education dept policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students — student-focused, intended reversal in 2026. So this sits above parent, similar to dossier 2 but slightly less comprehensive? Dossier 2 has explicit facilities access protected by law and top protective ranking plus refuge protections. Dossier 4 has low-risk group, protections across areas. I'd give dossier 4 ~0.55 and dossier 2 ~0.58. Actually dossier 4's protections are strong: public accommodations, hate crime, panic repeal, easy documents, low-risk ranking, one high court ruling on school bathroom. Maybe 0.55.

Dossier 5: Oklahoma-like — explicitly named (oops, "Oklahoma" appears — but we shouldn't guess country; it's given in text so fine). Most restrictive: facility ban K-12 (2022, 2025), executive order defining sex applying to state facilities including bathrooms, incarceration; birth certificate changes banned, supreme court ruling retroactive; care ban for adults too in public facilities (SB 904); no state anti-discrimination; hate crime law lacks gender identity; sports bans; death threats case; grading not stated but among most restrictive. This is worse than parent substantially. Also the state's own executive order applies to incarceration — visitor could be detained. Universal exposure: state-owned facility bathroom restrictions — executive order applies to all state-owned facilities (bathrooms/changing rooms), which a visitor may encounter (courthouses, state parks, DMV). Tier 1-ish. Score maybe 0.22-0.25. Dossier 3 has no adult facility restriction documented (school only), but anti-discrimination withdrawal and worst-group tier. Dossier 5 adds adult care ban in public facilities (resident), state facility bathroom order covering all state facilities (visitor-facing), no hate crime coverage, no discrimination protection, plus a documented death-threats case (dated 2018). So 5 is lowest: ~0.22. Dossier 3: ~0.27. Dossier 1: ~0.33.

Let me double check dossier 1 vs parent 0.35. Dossier 1 second-highest of five tiers (so tier 4 of 5, with four jurisdictions worse... actually "second-highest of five tiers, beneath the four jurisdictions graded highest risk"). It has a school/college facility law (visitor-facing if on campus), narrowed driver's license markers (Aug 2026: M/F only, exact-matching birth certificate or passport — affects residents; visitors' foreign docs). Outing of trans candidates from ballot (local sphere). Some positives: 33 municipal non-discrimination ordinances, employment protections. Roughly parent-level, slightly below or at. 0.33 or 0.34. I'll say 0.33.

Hmm, but dossier 1's facility law covers K-12 and colleges including private — universal exposure on campuses only. Dossier 5's executive order covers all state-owned facilities — broader. Dossier 3's school rule covers everyone on school grounds.

Dossier 4 vs 2: Both well above parent. Dossier 2: "most protective," top bands, facilities protected (2023 law full access bathroom for all genders), refuge protections (shield-like), hate crime conviction precedent, court orders hospital to resume care. Dossier 4: low-risk group, protections enacted 2020, X marker, documents accessible, but administrative school policies (2023) and athletics association ban (2025) — youth only. Dossier 4 lacks documented facilities protection statute but also lacks documented facility ban for adults (unverified list). I'd put 2 at 0.58, 4 at 0.54.

Note the parent national passport regime applies to all — none can exceed maybe 0.60 given the national entry/document exposure (universal: passport markers, visa cable with discrepancy refusal, foreign advisories). So cap around 0.60.

Final: 1: 0.33, 2: 0.58, 3: 0.27, 4: 0.54, 5: 0.22.

Check ordering logic: 5 < 3 < 1 < 4 < 2. Reasonable.
